chapters.title: Chapter 4: Property, Unlisted Shares and Foreign Assets

lessons.title: US Stocks and Foreign Funds: Capital Gains for Indian Residents

body.text: As an Indian resident, your gains on Apple, Nvidia or a US ETF are taxed in India, in rupees, as if the shares were unlisted. The rupee's fall adds to your taxable gain, and the reporting rules can cost more than the tax if you ignore them.

children.text: Aditi, a 30-year-old software engineer in Hyderabad, invests in US stocks through an overseas investing app and also receives RSUs from her employer's US parent. She assumed US shares were taxed like Indian shares: 12 months to long-term and a ₹1.25 lakh exemption. Both assumptions were wrong, and she had never filled in Schedule FA.

body.caption: Four ways Indians get US market exposure, and how each is taxed (tax year 2026-27)

cells: US stocks and US-listed ETFs bought directly through an overseas broker
Long-term 12.5%; short-term slab rate; no ₹1.25 lakh exemption
RSUs or ESPP shares from a foreign employer
Salary tax at vesting, then as direct US stocks
International funds of funds from Indian fund houses
No, they are Indian mutual fund units
International ETFs listed on NSE or BSE

body.title: The 14-Month Nvidia Sale
body.question: Aditi bought Nvidia shares directly through her US broker and sells them after 14 months at a profit. How is the gain taxed?
options: Long-term at 12.5% above the ₹1.25 lakh exemption
Not taxed in India because the shares are held abroad
body.explanation: Foreign shares are not listed on a recognised Indian exchange, so they run on the 24-month clock. At 14 months the gain is short-term and added to her income at slab rate. The ₹1.25 lakh exemption is only for Indian listed equity with STT. As a resident, her worldwide gains are taxable in India.

children.text: Your Gain Is Measured in Rupees

markDefs.definition: The telegraphic transfer buying rate of a foreign currency published by State Bank of India. Rule 115 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 uses this rate on a specified date to convert foreign currency income into rupees.

children.text: Indian tax is computed in rupees. The Income-tax Rules use the

on the last day of the month before the relevant month. In common practice, your cost is converted at the rate for the purchase month and your sale value at the rate for the sale month. That means a weaker rupee adds to your taxable gain even if the share price has not moved.

body.title: Convert and Compute
body.prompt: Using the table above, Aditi's cost is $1,700 at ₹82.70 and her sale value is $2,300 at ₹87.50. What is her capital gain in rupees?
body.explanation: Sale value = $2,300 × ₹87.50 = ₹2,01,250. Cost = $1,700 × ₹82.70 = ₹1,40,590. Gain = ₹60,660. Her dollar gain was only $600; the rupee's fall added the rest.

body.text: The conversion method is not fully settled. Some professionals read Rule 115 as requiring you to compute the gain in dollars first and convert only that gain at the rate for the sale month. On Aditi's numbers, that gives ₹52,500 instead of ₹60,660. The separate-conversion method shown above is the one most brokers, apps and practitioners use. Pick a method with your tax adviser and apply it consistently.

children.text: RSUs are taxed like ESOPs from the previous lesson, with a currency layer. When they vest, the FMV of the shares in rupees is taxed as salary and your employer deducts TDS, often by selling some shares to cover it. That rupee FMV becomes your cost, and the 24-month clock starts from the vesting or allotment date.

body.title: Aditi Sells RSUs Too Early
body.scenario: 40 RSUs vested for Aditi when the share price was $150 and the applicable rate was ₹85.00. Ten months later she sells all 40 shares at $175, with a sale-month rate of ₹87.50. She is in the 30% slab.
body.prompt: What was taxed at vesting, what is her capital gain, and at what rate?
body.modelAnswer: At vesting, 40 × $150 × ₹85.00 = ₹5,10,000 was added to her salary and taxed at slab rate through TDS. That ₹5,10,000 is her cost for capital gains. Sale value = 40 × $175 × ₹87.50 = ₹6,12,500. Capital gain = ₹1,02,500. She held the shares for only 10 months against a 24-month clock, so the gain is short-term and taxed at her 30% slab: ₹30,750 before cess. Her employer's payroll records of vest dates and FMV are essential for this calculation.

children.text: Tax Already Paid in the US

body.title: Dividends vs Capital Gains on US Shares

columns.label: Dividends
points: US withholding capped at 25% under the India-US tax treaty, once you submit Form W-8BEN
Taxable in India at your slab rate in rupees
US tax withheld can be claimed as foreign tax credit in India
File Form 67 before your ITR to claim the credit (renamed Form 44 under the new Income-tax Rules)

columns.label: Capital Gains
points: Generally not taxed by the US for Indian residents who are not US persons
Taxed only in India, at 12.5% or slab rate depending on holding period
No foreign tax credit needed because no US tax is paid
Report sale details in Schedule CG and holdings in Schedule FA

children.text: The Reporting Rules That Catch People

markDefs.definition: The foreign assets schedule in ITR-2 and ITR-3 where residents and ordinarily residents disclose foreign shares, bank and broker accounts, RSUs and other foreign assets held at any time during the calendar year.

children.text: If you are resident and ordinarily resident, you must report every foreign asset in
of ITR-2 or ITR-3, including shares, broker cash balances and unvested or vested RSUs. ITR-1 cannot be used once you hold foreign assets.

body.title: Which Year Does Schedule FA Follow?
body.textWithBlank: Schedule FA asks for foreign assets held at any time during the ___ year ending 31 December, not the financial year.
body.explanation: Capital gains follow the tax year from April to March, but foreign asset disclosure follows the calendar year from January to December. Shares you bought and sold within the year still need to be reported.

body.label: Penalty for Not Reporting Foreign Assets
body.context: Under the Black Money Act. Since 1 October 2024, the penalty does not apply if the total value of undisclosed foreign assets other than immovable property is ₹20 lakh or less, but the obligation to disclose remains.

stats.label: LRS limit
stats.context: Per person per financial year for permitted remittances

stats.label: TCS on investment remittances
stats.context: On the amount above ₹10 lakh in a financial year

stats.label: TCS is refundable
stats.context: Adjusted against your tax in the ITR, not an extra tax

stats.label: ITR form
stats.context: Required once you hold foreign assets

body.title: Deep Dive: US Estate Tax and the Indian-Listed Alternative

children.text: US estate tax is not an income tax, but it matters for Indian investors holding US shares directly. Non-US persons have only a small estate tax exemption on US-situated assets such as US shares, so heirs of a large US portfolio can face US estate tax on death. India and the US do not have an estate tax treaty.

Indian international funds of funds and NSE-listed international ETFs hold the foreign shares inside an Indian fund structure. You do not report them in Schedule FA and do not face US estate tax on them, though you give up direct ownership and may face tracking differences or fund-level limits on overseas investment.

cards.definition: Not listed in India, so 24-month clock, 12.5% long-term, slab rate short-term, no ₹1.25 lakh exemption.
SBI telegraphic transfer buying rate, used to convert foreign currency amounts into rupees for tax.
Rupee FMV at vesting that was taxed as salary.
Filed before the ITR to claim foreign tax credit, such as US tax withheld on dividends. Form 44 under the new Rules.
Foreign asset disclosure for the calendar year, mandatory for residents and ordinarily residents.
20% on investment remittances above ₹10 lakh a year, claimable as a credit in your ITR.

body.title: Year-End Checklist for US Investors
steps: Download your broker's annual transaction report and dividend statement for the tax year and the calendar year
Convert each purchase and sale using SBI TT buying rates and keep the rate sheet
Split gains into short-term (24 months or less) and long-term
Collect RSU vest confirmations showing dates, FMV and shares sold to cover tax
File Form 67 for US tax withheld on dividends before filing your ITR
Complete Schedule FA for every foreign account and holding during the calendar year, and claim any TCS in your return

points: Residents are taxed in India on gains from foreign shares, which follow the 24-month clock and get no ₹1.25 lakh exemption
Long-term gains are taxed at 12.5% and short-term gains at slab rate
Gains are computed in rupees using SBI TT buying rates, so rupee depreciation increases taxable gains
RSUs are taxed as salary at vesting, and that rupee FMV becomes your cost
US dividend withholding can be claimed as a credit through Form 67, while capital gains are generally taxed only in India
Schedule FA disclosure is mandatory on a calendar-year basis, with a ₹10 lakh penalty for non-disclosure above the ₹20 lakh threshold

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not tax or investment advice. Share prices and exchange rates used are illustrative, not actual SBI TT buying rates. Sections, rates and thresholds reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 and related laws for tax year 2026-27. Foreign investing involves tax, reporting and estate issues in more than one country, so consult a qualified tax professional before acting.
